title: Sage Vishvamitra's Request
captions: King Dasharatha hurried to welcome the sage Vishvamitra and bowed low before him.
“Great sage, your visit is a blessing,” said the king. “Ask for anything, and I promise it shall be yours.”
“Demons keep spoiling my sacred fire ceremony in the forest,” said Vishvamitra. “Send your son Rama with me to protect it.”
The king's heart sank. “Rama is still a boy! Take me and my whole army, but please do not ask for my son.”
Then the wise Vasishtha spoke gently. “A king must keep his word. Trust the sage. Rama will be safe, and he will learn great things.”
Dasharatha took a deep breath and kept his promise. He blessed Rama and Lakshmana and placed them in the sage's care.
With bows on their shoulders, the two young princes followed Vishvamitra out of Ayodhya and into their first great adventure.
story: One day the great sage Vishvamitra arrived at the palace of Ayodhya. Vishvamitra had once been a mighty king, and through long years of tapas he had become one of the greatest rishis in the world. King Dasharatha hurried out to welcome him and bowed low.
The king was so happy to see him that he made a big promise. “Your visit is a blessing,” he said. “Ask for anything, and it shall be yours.”
Vishvamitra explained his trouble. Whenever he performed a sacred fire ceremony in the forest, demons came and spoiled it. He asked the king to send Rama with him to protect it.

The king's heart sank. Rama was still young, and Dasharatha could not bear to send him into danger. He begged the sage to take him and his whole army instead. Vishvamitra grew angry, because the king was going back on his word.

Then the wise Vasishtha spoke gently to the king. He reminded him that a king of the Ikshvaku line must always keep his word, and that Rama would be safe with Vishvamitra and would learn great things. Dasharatha took a deep breath and kept his promise. He blessed Rama and Lakshmana, and the two princes followed the sage out of Ayodhya.
lesson: King Dasharatha loved Rama more than his own life, so keeping his promise was very hard. But in our tradition a promise is sacred. Satya means speaking the truth and doing what you said you would do, even when it is difficult. The king kept his word, and he trusted his guru's advice.
lesson_long: Satya means truth. It means speaking honestly, and it also means doing what you said you would do.

King Dasharatha loved Rama more than his own life, so this promise was very hard to keep. For a moment he wanted to take it back. But he listened to his guru, remembered who he was and kept his word. As the Ramayana goes on, we will see again and again how much this family values a promise.
Our elders teach that a promise is like a seed. Once it is planted, we care for it until it grows, even when that takes courage.
tradition: The Mundaka Upanishad says satyameva jayate, which means truth alone wins. These words are the national motto of India and are written below its national emblem.

The kings of Ayodhya belonged to the family of King Raghu, and they were famous for keeping their word. A well loved line from the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas says that in Raghu's family, people would rather give up their life than break a promise.
words: a great sage who sees deep truths
long, focused prayer and self discipline
a sacred fire ceremony with prayers and offerings
question: Have you ever made a promise that was hard to keep? What did you do?
questions: Have you ever made a promise that was hard to keep? What did you do?
Why did Vasishtha tell the king to keep his promise?
Is it better to make fewer promises and keep them all? Why?
card_lesson: The king's promise was very hard to keep, but he kept it. Satya means speaking the truth and doing what you said you would do, even when it is difficult.
